text:
sara: Quick idea — can we explore a zero-copy streaming surface for the Go SDK that behaves like an io.Reader so apps can pipe token streams directly into processors?

jason: I sketched something a while back: generator returns a Reader but we ended up copying due to auth/retry boundary.

priya: FWIW the auth refresh path is the tricky bit. If a request fails mid-stream and we retry, we need a way to resume without re-emitting tokens to the app.

sara: Right. Goal is minimal allocations for large streaming workloads (semantic search ingest, realtime assistants). Getting parity with other SDKs would be great.

jason: rough sketch: 
```go
type StreamReader interface {
    io.Reader
    Close() error
    // Seq returns the last-emitted sequence number for resume/dup-detection
    Seq() int64
}
// server frames: [seq:uint64][payload_len:uint32][payload bytes]
```

priya: Sequence numbers are good. But runtime needs to guarantee idempotent frames on retry. If we resend from seq N, we must ensure downstream dedup.

marco: Can we piggyback a short resumable handshake on the websocket/tcp layer? e.g., client-sends-last-received-seq and server truncates/rewinds the stream accordingly. That avoids needing the app to buffer.

sara: That sounds promising. Does it work with our existing token-caching & KV prefix caching?

priya: It interacts badly with our KV cache right now — we prefill KV and then stream tokens. If we replay tokens after an auth refresh, the cached state may diverge. Need an explicit checkpoint hook: runtime commit cache at seq X.

jason: Implementation note: make the Reader return ErrWouldRetry (or a sentinel) when a transient auth occurs so higher layers can call ResumeFrom(seq). Helps sample apps be explicit.

priya: Also consider backpressure: io.Reader blocks the goroutine. For high-throughput apps we want non-blocking pull with context cancellation. Maybe provide both Pull() chan and Reader adaptor.

marco: Perf tradeoffs: Reader path avoids allocations but forces sync scheduling. Channel path is lock-free but allocates goroutines. We can provide both and docs recommending Reader for simple piping, Pull for high concurrency.

jason: I can prototype Reader + ResumeFrom in the sample app. Will add a small harness that simulates auth token rotation and transient 401 mid-stream.

sara: Love it. Can you also add a tiny guide in the sample app about how to detect duplicate tokens using Seq()? New hires keep getting confused by replays.

jason: yep. I'll PR the sample to devex/sdks/go-samples/stream-zero-copy with tests.

priya: CI note: if you add integration tests, stub the runtime to emit identical sequence frames so we can assert no duplicates.

ci-bot: build failed on the last run: runtime/resume tests flaked (timeout). Log: 
```
--- FAIL: TestResume (0.00s)
    resume_test.go:48: expected 150 tokens, got 300 (duplicate emission)
```

marco: That log lines up with the bug where replay didn't cut KV. We'll need the resume handshake to also trigger a cache rollback/restore.

jason: Plan: prototype API + sample app, wire a test harness that simulates mid-stream 401s, then iterate on runtime checkpoint API. I'll target a draft PR by EOD Friday.

sara: Awesome. Thanks — can you add a short README snippet explaining why Reader vs Channel? New engineers ask about this daily :eyes:

jason: will do. Also adding a small snippet showing how to wrap the Reader into a scanner for token-by-token processing.

priya: One more UX nit: if we return sentinel ErrWouldRetry, standard io.Readers will choke. Consider returning a small error type implementing error and a helper function IsRetry(err) to keep ergonomics good.

jason: good call. I'll design the error so fmt.Printf still looks reasonable but IsRetry() is available.

sara: Thanks team — follow up in the PR thread. :thumbsup:
